That’s who we were listening to, we were sitting there on the floor. “‘These boogers [come], when somebody is in bed, sick. They say these boogers bother them,’ she said,” he said. That’s what they were saying when they were talking about it. “‘On the house, the corner, there were four little boogers perched,’ she said. ‘The biggest one, that’s where it had a place, sitting. That’s when the sick person has trouble breathing. They used the hair and wrapped it around here [gestures] and there [gestures] and when they pull it, that’s when they have trouble breathing. The sick person,’ that’s what she said, telling whoever was listening to her.” My dad’s brother, Tsal(i) was his name. He was sitting nearby, too, listening to the old woman. “How do you know what the boogers were doing? Is that what you do, too?” he said to her. “You be quiet! You are asking rude questions!” she said to him. She scolded him for talking about her.

phrases.english_text: That Ned Longbird she’s talking about, he was always walking on the road. He was always picking up anything on the road, no matter how hot it was! And he’d have on a big coat. He’ll have things in a bag. We lived nearby and when he came and we’d be sitting, my late father would say hello. Ned would come up to the porch and go inside the house. If there was something there, like bread, he would take it all and come back out and go on. [laughter] “Yeah, come back again!” Dad would tell him. That’s how Ned Longbird was. He was a good person and he was old, but he was walking good on the road. He would pick anything up on the road and put it in his pocket ’cause he had on a big coat all the time.

phrases.english_text: It would be all night! Nowadays, it has to be far away before you can spend the night. Back then, if they lived in walking distance, you would spend the night. There was an old man named Diganotsatl(i) who lived there. We lived way up on the hill from him. We would go there with our mom. We would spend the night. When they said, “You all spend the night here!” we would spend the night. There was a man named Tsusolvd(i). He was Diganotsatl(i)’s son. He said, “Lillie! Let’s just lie here! If the rooster crows, it’ll be sitting right above us! I just hope it don’t poop on you!” he said. “Haw!” I told him. I was laying real close to him, him with his overalls on. He didn’t even take his overalls off. Me and Tsusolvd(i) were in bed. And then in the morning, the rooster crowed. There was a board across there, because there was no wall, just sheetrock. That’s where the rooster was standing, right above where I was laying. I got up. I thought it was going to poop on me! They thought it was funny, and they laughed at me.

phrases.english_text: That’s how we were something. We lived closer this way. I remember, sometimes we were all scattered laying, sleeping outside on the porch in the summer. This [gestures] way lived the late Nellie Mays. She lived there with her husband, Gill Mayes. That’s who would wake us up on the porch in the mornings. He’d be there early in the morning, on horseback. “Wake up, wake up!” he’d say. “Time to get up!” he’d say. Gill Fay Mayes.
